video_title: Is Bitcoin Ready To Rip While Wall Street Breaks?
gist: Jordi Visser argues the AI-driven hedge fund sell-off resembles LTCM-style deleveraging rather than an AI bubble pop, with tokenization and Bitcoin as the long-run beneficiaries and Fed/CPI as irrelevant. He and Pompliano then debate whether Anthropic's growth decelerates as open-source models and falling token prices spread.

insights.claim: Visser argues hedge funds are the only leveraged part of the system being knocked out, comparable to LTCM, because funds are betting on how long investors stay and how long prime brokers keep extending leverage.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Leverage purge in crowded AI trades is a positioning/timing risk, not evidence the AI buildout is failing.
insights.quote: You are making a bet as to how long your investors will stay with you.

insights.claim: Lone Pine Capital reportedly was up 40%+ in the first half and gave back the entire gain by end of September while the S&P was up only about 2% in the quarter and the VIX barely moved.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Shows a drawdown driven by crowding and leverage rather than broad market stress.

insights.claim: Visser says multistrat/pod hedge funds depend on convert and long-short spreads not widening; convert-related positions (including CoreWeave and MicroStrategy converts) and a September biotech blowup caused another LTCM-style spread widening.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Relative-value spread blowouts can force selling of fundamentally sound assets.

insights.claim: Concentration of AI winners is so small and losers so large that deleveraging will persist, leaving investors needing to bet on certainty with a time component; anyone needing the AI positions to work within a month is in trouble.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Favor patience and unlevered exposure over short-horizon leveraged AI bets.

insights.claim: Visser says he stayed out of the hedge fund industry because he does not want to compete against AI agents; he claims an AI agent can now do everything a hedge fund does, including risk management and 13F crowding checks.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Implies structural fee and alpha compression for discretionary and quant funds.
insights.quote: I have no interest in being in a competition against artificial intelligence

insights.claim: Morgan Stanley prime brokerage data cited to Visser shows the AI long-short trade in the 7th percentile of the last year, which he reads as risk being fully taken off and a setup for the next AI bounce.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Washed-out positioning is a contrarian entry signal for AI-linked equities.

themes.theme: AI financing: CoreWeave is not telecom

insights.claim: Visser contends the AI buildout differs from the dot-com telecom bust because capital comes from Microsoft, OpenAI, Meta and similar large payers rather than weak borrowers, and he notes no defaults from them; CoreWeave demand is sold out to 2030 per Gartner as he describes it.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Counterparty quality supports the neocloud credit thesis versus a housing/telecom analogy.

insights.claim: Visser says as long as compute demand exceeds supply there is no chance of an unwind like the dot-com bubble, but the equity/bond investment merit of CoreWeave is unknown and will not be clear until roughly 2028-2030.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Separates the inevitability of AI compute from the investability of specific financed names.

insights.claim: Visser argues the CDS blowouts and correlation in non-winner AI names stem from the concentration of capital issuance (Broadcom, Google, OpenAI, Anthropic, SpaceX each raising huge amounts) hitting the same portfolios, not from bad trades.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: A supply-of-paper indigestion story implies recovery once profits delever positions.

insights.claim: Pompliano relays that Paul Tudor Jones said 2027 would be a negative-liquidity year with many companies coming to market; Visser disagrees that the market necessarily goes down but says investors must be patient.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Heavy equity issuance supply is a flagged risk window for liquidity.

insights.claim: Visser says he has total confidence that over three years a basket of semiconductors, optical and data-center industrial companies will see earnings and outperform homebuilders and autos, but timing any single month is hard because hedge funds are crowded in the same trades.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Basket exposure over multi-year horizon rather than timing entry.

insights.claim: Visser argues tokenization will free trapped capital in private credit, private equity, VC and endowments by creating clearing prices, and would shift flows from vintage 2021-22 SaaS private credit toward assets like CoreWeave debt at 75 cents on the dollar.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Price discovery in illiquid assets could redirect capital and pressure alternatives managers.

insights.claim: Visser says most private credit holdings are 2021-22 SaaS loans that AI is eroding, and BDCs trade about 20% below where retail private credit investors are marked.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Marks may reset lower as AI disrupts software borrowers.

insights.claim: Visser thinks tokenization enabling 24/7, 365 risk management will change volatility, hedging and prime brokers' ability to provide leverage, which he says would hit hedge funds even though mega funds with five-year lockups last longest.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Structural threat to hedge fund business models over time, not necessarily this year.

insights.claim: Visser says Bitcoin was up close to 30% and Ethereum more than 30% since June while the S&P and Nasdaq were flat, with Bitcoin holding roughly $82,000-$85,000 during the AI sell-off, which he attributes to a standout Sharpe ratio.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Bitcoin showing relative strength in a stressed tape.

insights.claim: Visser expects Bitcoin's next move up to the highs to coincide with the next AI bounce, around the hyperscaler earnings, end of October or December, but sees the main crypto upside in the next year as tokenization draws attention and money.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Gives a catalyst calendar linking crypto to AI risk-on.

insights.claim: Visser thinks the hedge against AI disruption is to buy Bitcoin, since few companies are safe from being disrupted, and sees agents choosing Bitcoin as a safe store of value in a deflationary world.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Frames Bitcoin as a non-disruptable asset rather than an inflation hedge.
insights.quote: You know what the hedge is? If I'm right, it's to go buy Bitcoin.

insights.claim: Pompliano frames the portfolio as AI is offense, Bitcoin is defense: use AI to generate revenue and profit, then store it in Bitcoin to protect from disruption.
insights.speaker: Anthony Pompliano
insights.so_what: Simple barbell allocation framework.
insights.quote: AI is offense, Bitcoin is defense.

insights.claim: Visser says he believes in accelerating deflation from AI, which upsets both the debasement crowd and the programmable-money crowd, and that leverage and high return hurdles become unnecessary in that world.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Deflation thesis conflicts with the standard debasement case for Bitcoin and gold.

insights.claim: Visser reframes Elon Musk's claim that SpaceX could be bigger than the global economy as the roughly $900 trillion of mostly illiquid assets moving through tokenization into liquid form, allowing a single 50 trillion company.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Tokenization TAM argument for extreme valuations.

insights.claim: Visser says CPI level (2.2% vs 3.2%) no longer matters for making money, citing that only about 24% of S&P 1500 stocks created alpha since ChatGPT, and that recession risk comes only from mass job loss and credit unwind, which he says will not happen.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Argues markets are driven by AI, not inflation prints.

insights.claim: Visser cites weekly jobless claims near 200,000, which he calls the lowest in history unadjusted and lower even after population adjustment, as evidence there is no job loss.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Labor data supports the no-recession stance.

insights.claim: Visser notes the S&P 500 has returned about 17% a year over 10 years and above 10% over every trailing window from 20 to 90 years, arguing compounding beats fear of bubbles.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Long-horizon base rate against bubble-calling.

insights.claim: Visser says this year's S&P rally lasted only about three months (March to June), driven by AI, and he thinks the AI trade works about three months a year so alpha windows are shrinking, as with Nvidia making money about 20% of the time.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Supports staying invested rather than timing short windows.

themes.theme: Anthropic, open source and the token economy

insights.claim: Pompliano argues Anthropic's growth will decelerate because of rising competition and falling token prices, using the identity tokens processed times price per token equals revenue, and cites Ramp AI index and OpenRouter open-source growth as evidence of share loss per customer.
insights.speaker: Anthony Pompliano
insights.so_what: Frontier lab revenue growth faces both volume-share and price pressure.
insights.quote: number of tokens processed times price per token equals revenue

insights.claim: Pompliano says his company Sylvia pays 97% less processing 500 million tokens on its own hardware and open-source models than on Anthropic, with better latency and accuracy, after compute costs rose to $550,000 per month in about five months.
insights.speaker: Anthony Pompliano
insights.so_what: Concrete example of small companies migrating off frontier APIs.

insights.claim: Pompliano predicts large enterprises such as JP Morgan will eventually prefer sovereign, fine-tuned open-source stacks for privacy, regulation and cost, with frontier labs serving as the starter pack for AI adoption.
insights.speaker: Anthony Pompliano
insights.so_what: Long-run margin pressure on closed-model vendors.

insights.claim: Visser agrees open source will win for digital-economy firms but argues enterprises will keep paying Anthropic and OpenAI for smarter intelligence and low risk, as Jensen Huang argued, and that frontier labs will dominate research and science while restricting distillation.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Barbell outcome: open source for commodity use, frontier labs for hard problems.

insights.claim: Pompliano proposes a 'fat model thesis' analogous to the failed fat protocol thesis in crypto, concluding value will be split across models, apps and infrastructure, perhaps with models capturing about 40%.
insights.speaker: Anthony Pompliano
insights.so_what: Argues for diversifying across the stack.

insights.claim: Visser says Anthropic would reach roughly 100 billion ARR by year end (about 10 times a year ago) and he expects around 3 to 3.5 times next year; Pompliano cites its implied valuation falling from about 2 trillion to 1.5 trillion.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Both agree growth slows from a 10x pace; figures are unverified in the discussion.

insights.claim: Visser argues Stripe's purchase of OpenRouter and AI agents moving cash to money-market funds threaten JP Morgan's net interest income of $107 billion, since money market funds have grown 70% since 2022 versus 56% for bank deposits.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Agentic yield-seeking could compress bank deposit spreads.

insights.claim: Pompliano suggests a possible Tesla-SpaceX merger, with SpaceX likely acquiring Tesla at a premium of perhaps 15-30%, could cause Tesla to grind higher into year end on hedge fund speculation, noting Elon Musk liked his tweet supporting it.
insights.speaker: Anthony Pompliano
insights.so_what: Speculative merger-premium trade based on a social media like and rumor.
